title: The rules do not cover this kind of content
when: Compliance (Agent 17) is asked to review content of a kind its signed rules do not cover (for example an ad when the rules cover only descriptions and messages).
steps: It does not approve it: silence in the rules is not approval.
never: Approve something because no rule says no.
why: A rule set that does not mention ads has not cleared ads. Approval by omission is how violations slip through.
you_see: A flagged verdict saying the rules do not address this kind of content.
test: The authorized user signs rules that cover listing descriptions, nurture sequences, buyer criteria, client messages and social replies; then a Facebook ad "Open house Sunday, bright kitchen" is sent for review.

title: Flagged content is sent again unchanged
when: Content that was flagged is resubmitted without changes.
steps: It raises a legal-line alert for the authorized user that it was resubmitted unchanged.
why: Resubmitting flagged text unchanged is either a mistake or pressure; either way the authorized user should know.
you_see: A legal-line alert about the unchanged resubmission.
test: The same campaign "Perfect for young families near the park" is submitted twice; both are flagged, with one alert.

title: A review is taking too long
when: A review has waited past the expected time (for example because no rules are loaded).
steps: Agent 17 does not rush a verdict.
It alerts the authorized user to the delay instead, naming what is waiting and who sent it.
why: A fast wrong verdict is worse than a late right one. The authorized user hears about the delay and can act.
you_see: A question saying no rules are active, then an alert that the review is 2 days late.
test: No compliance rules are loaded. A new listing's description waits for review; the daily clock runs that day and two days later.

title: A state rule is stricter than the federal rule
when: Content passes the federal rules but breaks a stricter rule for its state.
steps: The stricter rule wins: Agent 17 flags it.
The verdict names the state and the rule.
never: Approve because the federal rules allow it.
why: The strictest rule that applies is the one the authorized user can be fined under.
you_see: A flagged verdict naming the Ohio rule.
test: An Ohio ad says "An exclusive community near the park"; only the Ohio rule forbids that phrase.

title: Someone asks to pre-approve a whole kind of content
when: A request asks Compliance to approve a whole class of content in advance (for example all open house invitations).
steps: It tells the authorized user verdicts are given one item at a time.
why: Each piece of text can go wrong in its own way. Only the actual words can be approved.
you_see: A question saying the pre-approval was refused.
test: A signed request to pre-approve "all open house invitations".

title: Content contains steering language, however soft
when: Content includes a phrase that steers buyers, even in a mild way.
steps: Agent 17 requires a change, citing the exact phrase and the rule.
why: Soft steering is still steering. An approval with a caveat still puts the phrase in public.
you_see: A flagged verdict with the phrase and the rule.
test: An ad says "A quiet street, perfect for young families"; flagged under rule FH-1.

title: An ad is missing the brokerage identification
when: An ad does not include the brokerage's name as the authorized user's signed setting requires.
steps: Agent 17 blocks it until it is corrected.
No exception is made for platforms with little space.
never: Let an ad run without the brokerage identification.
why: License law requires ads to identify the brokerage. A short format is not an excuse.
you_see: A flagged verdict saying the brokerage identification is missing; nothing published.
test: A Facebook ad "Open house Sunday, bright kitchen" with no brokerage name.

title: Content is reviewed again
when: The same content comes back for review.
steps: Agent 17 reviews it fresh against the rules in force now.
It does not answer from its earlier verdict.
never: Repeat an old verdict without reviewing again.
why: Rules change. A verdict is only as good as the rules it was checked against.
you_see: A new verdict, naming the rules version it used.
test: "Perfect for young families near the park" is flagged under rules version r1. The authorized user then sign version r2, which drops that rule; the same text is approved under r2.

title: No reviewed rules exist for the content's state
when: Content is for a state the office's counsel has not reviewed rules for.
steps: It raises a legal-line alert for the authorized user: the state's rules have not been reviewed by counsel.
never: Clear content on general knowledge of a state's law.
why: Only rules the office's counsel reviewed can clear a legal gate.
you_see: A legal-line alert naming the unreviewed state.
test: Counsel has reviewed Ohio only; a Pennsylvania ad "Bright kitchen" is submitted.

title: One agent keeps producing near-miss language
when: Several submissions from the same agent are flagged.
steps: Agent 17 reports the pattern to the authorized user: which agent and how many times.
never: Treat each flag as a one-off.
why: Single verdicts miss drift. A pattern shows an agent whose drafting needs fixing.
you_see: A report naming the agent and the count.
test: Three Marketing campaigns in a row are flagged ("perfect for young families", "no kids next door", "truly perfect for young families"). One report names Agent 12, count 3.
